extracted.intended_audience: graduate and advanced undergraduate students studying algebraic geometry (Math 216)
extracted.subtask_description: Exercises, definitions, and theorems about intersection products, asymptotic Riemann–Roch, projection formulas, intersection theory on surfaces, Hodge Index, Grothendieck group K(X), and the Nakai–Moishezon/Kleiman ampleness criteria in a textbook setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multilinearity and very ample reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: By multilinearity of the intersection product, and the fact that each Ln may be written as the 'difference' of two very ample invertible sheaves (Exercise 16.6.C), it suffices to prove many intersection statements when the involved line bundles are very ample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique/hint: reduce general intersection computations to the very ample case by writing line bundles as differences of very ample ones; choose sections avoiding associated points when needed (see Exercise 16.6.C and use Exercise 20.1.C in inductive arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic Riemann–Roch (Exercise 20.1.I)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is projective, F is a coherent sheaf with dim Supp F = n, and L a line bundle on X, then χ(X, L^{⊗m} ⊗ F) is a polynomial in m of degree at most n. The coefficient of m^n (the leading term) is (L^n · F)/n!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: Use Exercise 20.1.H to show certain higher intersections vanish, expand using (20.1.1.1) to get a recursion for χ, and compare with the proof of polynomiality of the Hilbert polynomial (Theorem 18.6.1). Exercise 18.6.C may help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection formula for same-dimension integral projective schemes (Exercise 20.1.J)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π: X1 → X2 is a (projective) morphism of integral projective schemes (over a field k) of the same dimension n, and L1,...,Ln are invertible sheaves on X2. Then (π^*L1 · ... · π^*Ln) = deg(X1/X2) · (L1 · ... · Ln). (First intersection on X1, second on X2.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: reduce to the case the Li are very ample by multilinearity; choose sections whose intersection lies in an open subset U where π has constant degree deg π. Use Exercise 9.3.G to find dense open over which π is finite and Useful Exercise 13.7.F to get local freeness of π_*O of rank d.

rubrics_metrics.name: General projection formula (Remark 20.1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X1 → X2 is a proper morphism and F a coherent sheaf on X1 with dim Supp F ≤ n, and L1,...,Ln are invertible sheaves on X2, then (π^*L1 · ... · π^*Ln · F) = (L1 · ... · Ln · π_*F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes Exercise 20.1.J. References given: [FGIKNV, B.15] and [Ko1, Prop. VI.2.11]. The text does not give a proof here because it is not used later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection with ample line bundles (Exercise 20.1.K)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a projective k-variety and L is an ample line bundle on X, then for any subvariety Y ⊂ X of dimension n, (L^n · Y) > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: reduce to L very ample (Proposition 20.1.3 and Theorem 16.6.2), then show (L^n · Y) equals the degree of Y in the projective embedding given by |L|. This positivity is the content that Nakai–Moishezon will later characterize ampleness by.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomological interpretation over C (20.1.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: When k = C, (L1 · ... · Ln · [Y]) can be interpreted cohomologically as c1(L1^{an}) ∪ ... ∪ c1(Ln^{an}) ∩ [Y^{an}] in H_{2*}(Y^{an}, Z); the first Chern class of a line bundle with divisor D corresponds to the class of D^{an}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: reduce to very ample case and to effective Cartier divisors restricting to effective divisors on Y; then use induction and Exercise 20.1.C. See Exercise 18.4.G for background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additive notation for line bundles (20.1.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write tensor product of invertible sheaves additively (so the tensor power corresponds to scalar multiples), which is useful because of multilinearity of intersection products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convention simplifies multilinear computations but can be confusing (people sometimes prefer to use divisors). The text will use additive notation in later sections (e.g., 20.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of intersection number for divisors on surfaces (Exercise/Definition 20.2.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: For effective divisors C and D on a regular projective surface X: (20.2.0.1) deg_C O_X(D)|_C = (O(C) · O(D)); (20.2.0.2) Euler characteristic definition; (20.2.0.3) symmetry deg_D O_X(C)|_D = (O(C)·O(D)); and (20.2.0.4) if C and D have no common components then (C·D) = h^0(C ∩ D, O_{C∩D}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four descriptions each have pros and cons: Euler characteristic form is algebraically powerful, degree definition is less obviously symmetric, and the local h^0 description is clearly local and geometric. Use whichever is most helpful for the problem at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection form on Picard group (20.2.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The intersection number induces a bilinear intersection form Pic X × Pic X → Z on a regular projective surface X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Asymptotic Riemann–Roch (Exercise 20.1.I) to see χ(X, O(nD)) is a quadratic polynomial in n; this links intersection pairing with Riemann–Roch for surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for computing intersection matrices and Picard groups (Exercises 20.2.C, 20.2.D, 20.2.F etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete computations: on P1 × P1, Pic ∼= Zℓ ⊕ Zm with intersection numbers ℓ·m = 1, ℓ^2 = m^2 = 0; on Bl_p P2, Pic generated by ℓ and e with ℓ^2 = 1, e^2 = -1, ℓ·e = 0; nef cone and effective cone descriptions follow from intersecting with curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints: use Exercise 20.2.A(b) or Euler characteristic descriptions; relate proper transforms and exceptional divisors; show nef/effective cones are spanned by classes detecting nonnegativity on generators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and recognition of (-1)-curves (20.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A (-1)-curve is a curve C ≅ P1 consisting of smooth points with self-intersection C·C = -1. Later this can be restated as 'C has normal bundle O(-1)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: exceptional divisor of blow-up has self-intersection -1. Use Exercise 21.2.H and Exercise 20.2.A(a) to interpret normal bundle criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nef cone generators by intersection tests (Exercise 20.2.F and related)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show certain classes generate the nef cone (e.g., ℓ and m on Bl_p P2), prove they pair nonnegatively with all effective curve classes; by intersecting with generators, demonstrate no class outside the cone is nef.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy: show candidate generators are nef (intersect nonnegatively with all irreducible curves); then show any class outside their cone has negative intersection with at least one curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiber self-intersection for fibrations (20.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → B is a morphism from a regular projective surface to a regular curve and F is a fiber, then F·F = 0; equivalently, the self-intersection of a fiber is zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: O_X(F) = π^*O_B(b) restricts to trivial line bundle on the fiber, so degree on the fiber is zero. Phrase properly if X not regular: (π^*O_B(b))^2 = 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal bundle to a section of Proj of a rank-2 bundle (Exercise 20.2.I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a rank-2 locally free sheaf V on C with short exact sequence 0 → S → V → Q → 0 corresponding to a section σ: C → P(V), the normal bundle to σ(C) in P(V) is isomorphic to Q^∨, and the self-intersection σ(C)^2 equals deg_C Q (Exercise 20.2.J).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints include reducing to S ≅ O_X by tensoring, analyzing local trivializations and transition functions gij for Q to compute how trivializations of the normal bundle differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hirzebruch surfaces Fn properties (20.2.8–20.2.P)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fn = Proj_{P1}(O ⊕ O(n)) is a P1-bundle over P1; Pic Fn generated by E and F with E^2 = -n, F^2 = 0, effective cone generated by E and F, every effective curve is a nonnegative linear combination of E and F, and E is unique curve of negative self-intersection when n<0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct local charts to compute Pic and intersection matrix; show OF has no base dependence; use moving curves (F moves, C moves) to deduce effective cone generators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of nef/effective cones to distinguish varieties (Exercise 20.2.Q/R)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare effective and nef cones and intersection pairings to show varieties (e.g., Hirzebruch surfaces Fn) are pairwise nonisomorphic; negative self-intersection behavior distinguishes cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute cones and intersection forms explicitly to find invariants; use uniqueness of curves with certain self-intersections as discriminants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hodge Index Theorem for surfaces (20.2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be an irreducible smooth surface over a field k, H an ample class with H^2 > 0, and L with L·H = 0. Then (a) L^2 ≤ 0, and (b) equality L^2 = 0 holds iff L is numerically trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background needed: definitions of N^1(X) and ρ(X) (18.4.10). Consequence: intersection form on N^1(X)_R has signature (1, ρ(X)-1). Proof uses vanishing results, Serre duality, Riemann–Roch, and asymptotic arguments (see 20.2.11–20.2.14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Index/signature interpretation (Exercise 20.2.U)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the Hodge Index Theorem, one deduces that the real vector space N^1(X)_R with intersection bilinear form has signature (1, ρ(X)-1) — the Hodge index gives the positive direction from ample classes and the rest negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate to Sylvester's law of inertia; count positive, zero, and negative signs in any orthogonal basis to identify the index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing and positivity lemmas used in Hodge Index proof (20.2.11–20.2.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If H is ample and M ≫ ω_X (i.e., M more positive than ω_X) then h^2(X, M) = 0 (via Serre duality). If L·H > 0 then for n ≫ 0, L^{⊗n} has a nonzero section (use Riemann–Roch for surfaces and vanishing of higher cohomology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Serre duality to reduce h^2 vanishing to nonexistence of sections of certain bundles; apply Riemann–Roch to show χ grows as (n^2/2)L^2 - n(L·K_X) + constant, so for n large h^0>0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and basic properties of Grothendieck group K(X) (20.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: K(X) (often K_0(X)) is the abelian group generated by [F] for coherent sheaves F, subject to [F] = [F'] if isomorphic and [F'] + [F''] = [F] for short exact sequences 0 → F' → F → F'' → 0. It is the universal construction of an operator on CohX that 'behaves well in exact sequences'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If X is proper, Euler characteristic χ gives a map χ: K(X) → Z. If X is integral, rank descends to K(X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtration and first Chern class operator on K(X) (20.3.2–20.3.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: K(X) is filtered by support dimension: K(X)≤d generated by sheaves supported in dimension ≤ d; A'_d(X) is the dth graded piece. For invertible L, define an operator (first Chern class action) c1(L): K(X) → K(X) sending K(X)≤d to K(X)≤d−1; on associated graded it becomes additive and corresponds to intersection action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 20.3.A: over projective X with infinite k, L· sends K(X)≤d to K(X)≤d−1 by writing L as difference of very ample bundles and choosing sections avoiding associated points. Note the action of Pic is not additive on K(X) but c1 becomes additive on the associated graded A'_*.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of intersection product via c1 action
rubrics_metrics.description: For F supported of dimension at most n and invertible sheaves L1,...,Ln, the intersection (L1 · ... · Ln · F) can be reinterpreted as c1(L1) ∩ ... ∩ c1(Ln) [F] in A'_*(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a homology-like theory where classes [Y] = [O_Y] lie in A'_d(X) for subvarieties Y of pure dimension d, making intersection theory act on these 'homology' classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functoriality: pushforward and pullback on K(X) (20.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a proper morphism π: X1 → X2, there is a pushforward π_*: K(X1) → K(X2) given by the alternating sum of higher direct images: π_*[F] = [π_*F] - [R^1π_*F] + ... which descends to A' groups; for flat morphisms pushforward is exact and yields maps shifting degree according to relative dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functoriality interacts with the first Chern class operators to yield projection formulas and is compatible with Chow groups and cohomology realizations when k = C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between A'_d(X) and Chow groups Ad(X) (20.3.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural surjection Ad(X) → A'_d(X). After tensoring with Q, this map is an isomorphism (Fulton Thms. 18.2 and 18.3). The kernel of the map may be torsion in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References: [F, Ex. 15.1.5], [SGA6, Exp. XIV], and examples where kernel has torsion (e.g., group E8 with 2-,3-,5-torsion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nakai–Moishezon criterion for ampleness (Theorem 20.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is an invertible sheaf on a projective k-scheme X and for every subvariety Y ⊂ X of dimension n we have (L^n · Y) > 0, then L is ample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: X need only be proper for the result. Consequences: ampleness is numerical and makes sense on N^1_Q(X); the ample Q-line bundles form an open cone in N^1_Q(X). The proof is by induction on dimension and uses asymptotic Riemann–Roch, vanishing, and base-point-freeness arguments (see 20.4.5 Steps 1–4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness of ample cone (Proposition 20.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ample cone in N^1_Q(X) is open: given an ample class [A], small rational perturbations [A] + ε_1[L1] + ... + ε_n[Ln] remain ample for sufficiently small |ε_i|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: choose Li forming a basis of N^1_Q(X), clear denominators so some powers are very ample, then use cone properties and additive notation to exhibit a neighborhood of A consisting of ample Q-line bundles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof steps for Nakai–Moishezon (20.4.5: Steps 2–4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2: For L satisfying positivity hypotheses, χ(X, L^m) grows like (m^n)(L^n)/n!, so for m≫0 H^0(X, L^m) ≠ 0. Step 3: For m≫0, L^m is globally generated (use exact sequences, vanishing on divisors, and inductive hypothesis). Step 4: A base-point-free line bundle positive on every curve is ample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sequences (20.4.5.1)-(20.4.5.3), Serre vanishing, long exact cohomology sequences, and the inductive hypothesis that L is ample on closed subvarieties. Final appeal: Exercise 18.4.L that base-point-free positive-on-curves implies ampleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kleiman's Theorem (20.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is projective and L is nef (numerically effective), then (L^{dim V} · V) ≥ 0 for every irreducible subvariety V ⊂ X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a key ingredient for Kleiman's numerical criterion. The theorem is proved by induction on dimension using a very ample H and polynomial P(t) = ((L + tH)^n · X) and analyzing its roots and coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and criteria about nef and ample cones (Exercises 20.4.B and Theorem 20.4.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Limit of ample classes is nef (if L + εH is ample for small ε>0 then L is nef). (b) If H is ample and L is nef then L + εH is ample for small ε>0, so nef + ample = ample. Theorem 20.4.7: For projective X, the nef cone is the closure of the ample cone, and the ample cone is the interior of the nef cone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Nakai–Moishezon for rational t and openness of ample cone; be aware parts of these statements require projectivity (some fail in the merely proper case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial method in Kleiman proof (20.4.D/E exercises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider P(t) = ((L + tH)^n · X) ∈ Q[t]. If P(0)<0 but P(t)>0 for large t (since L + tH ample for t≫0), then P(t) has positive real roots; analyze the largest positive root t0 and use Nakai–Moishezon to deduce contradictions showing (L^n · X) ≥ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 20.4.D shows nonconstant coefficients of P(t) are nonnegative; Exercise 20.4.E uses Nakai–Moishezon to show (L + tH) is ample for rational t > t0. This formal polynomial argument underlies Kleiman's positivity conclusion.
